body:
Why political authority is difficult to identify

Political authority refers to the power to make and implement decisions affecting a community. In an urban society, such decisions may concern construction, public facilities, resource distribution, trade and the organisation of labour.

Harappan settlements demonstrate considerable coordination. However, the individuals or institutions responsible for that coordination have not been securely identified.

Unlike civilisations where readable inscriptions name kings, the Harappan civilisation has not provided accepted written records identifying its rulers.

Evidence of organised decision-making

Standardised construction

Harappan settlements used bricks with remarkably consistent proportions across a large geographical area. A common brick proportion was 1:2:4 for height, breadth and length.

This standardisation suggests widely accepted construction practices and some degree of coordination across settlements.

Planned settlements

Large Harappan cities contained organised streets, drainage arrangements, platforms and substantial public structures.

The construction of such buildings required workers, materials and decisions about where structures should be located.

Large walls and platforms also required the organisation of considerable labour. The successful completion of these structures indicates the capacity to coordinate collective activity.

Standardised weights

The Harappans used carefully manufactured weights, commonly cubical and made of chert.

The smaller weight denominations generally followed a binary progression, including 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16. Larger denominations incorporated decimal relationships.

Such standardisation was useful in exchange because people in different places could employ comparable measures.

Seals and the movement of goods

Seals could be pressed onto wet clay attached to tied packages. The resulting impression is called a sealing.

An intact sealing could indicate that a package had not been opened during transportation. It could also convey information about the sender or the movement of goods.

This practice provides evidence of organised exchange, although it does not identify the political authority supervising trade.

Was there a Harappan king?

No individual has been securely identified as a Harappan king.

A large building at Mohenjodaro was once described as a palace, but it lacked the unmistakable royal evidence needed to confirm that interpretation.

Likewise, a well-known stone sculpture of a bearded man has traditionally been called the priest-king.

The sculpture depicts an apparently important male figure wearing a decorated garment. Its identification as a priest or king, however, has not been established.

The name was influenced partly by comparisons with other ancient civilisations in which rulers sometimes possessed religious authority.

The priest-king is not a confirmed ruler

The existence of the sculpture is certain. Its identification as a priest, king or priest-king is not. The title is a conventional name for the artefact, not proof of the political office held by the person depicted.

Competing interpretations of Harappan government

Different explanations have been proposed for Harappan political organisation.

InterpretationMain reasoningLimitation
Centralised authorityShared standards and coordinated urban planningNo securely identified central ruler
Multiple local authoritiesLarge cities may have managed their own affairsExact administrative boundaries are unknown
Collective decision-makingCommunities may have coordinated important activitiesDecision-making institutions are not identified

A centralised political system is one possible explanation for widespread standardisation, but it is not the only explanation.

Similarly, uncertainty about kingship does not establish that all Harappans enjoyed equal political power.

Gujarat connection: Dholavira

Dholavira, situated on Khadir Island in the Rann of Kutch, provides important evidence of urban organisation.

The city contained a strongly fortified Castle, a Middle Town and a Lower Town, with substantial walls and distinct internal areas.

It also possessed sophisticated reservoirs and water-management structures. These required coordinated planning, construction and maintenance.

The organisation of Dholavira suggests that some form of administrative authority was involved in managing the settlement. Its specific political structure remains uncertain.

Its architectural divisions should therefore not be treated as proof of a particular monarchy, priesthood or hereditary ruling class.

Prelims focus

  • Harappan bricks commonly followed the proportion 1:2:4 for height, breadth and length.
  • Standardised weights, seals and construction practices suggest coordinated organisation.
  • Harappan weights were commonly made of chert.
  • The identity of Harappan rulers remains unknown.
  • The Mohenjodaro priest-king sculpture is not proof of a priestly monarchy.
  • Dholavira in Gujarat had a distinctive fortified settlement divided into major zones.
  • Trap: Evidence of planning does not establish that the entire civilisation was governed by 1 king.

[Sources: NCERT, Class 12, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Theme 1, Sections 3, 7 and 8, pp. 5–8 and 15–17; NCERT, Class 6, Exploring Society: India and Beyond, Chapter 6, pp. 90–96 and 100–101; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Dholavira: a Harappan City, Brief Synthesis and Statement of Outstanding Universal Value, consulted 17 November 2026.]

title: Political Authority Without Identified Kings

body:
What do Harappan images reveal?

Harappan settlements have yielded terracotta figurines, stone sculptures, bronze figures, seals and decorated pottery. Many display human forms, animals, plants or other symbolic designs.

Some of these objects may have served religious purposes. Others may have been used for decoration, play, identification or exchange.

The difficulty is that an image may carry a meaning that cannot be recovered from its appearance alone.

Female terracotta figurines

Numerous terracotta figurines depicting women have been recovered from Harappan sites. Some are heavily ornamented and wear elaborate headdresses.

Early interpretations identified several such figures as representations of a Mother Goddess.

The proposed connection was with fertility, motherhood and the growth of life. A female figure associated with plant imagery could, for example, be interpreted as symbolising fertility.

However, the identification is not certain.

Female figurines could have served different functions, and not every female representation should be assumed to depict a goddess.

The term Mother Goddess is an interpretation applied to certain Harappan figurines. Their existence is established, but their precise religious identity and use remain uncertain.

Other human figurines

Harappan art includes male and female human representations made from different materials.

The famous bronze figure called the Dancing Girl from Mohenjodaro is an important example of Harappan craftsmanship. Its conventional name reflects an interpretation of the figure's posture; it does not establish a religious identity or prove the profession of the person represented.

Similarly, the bearded stone bust known as the priest-king cannot be securely identified as a ruler or religious official.

Seals and animal representations

Harappan seals were commonly made from steatite, a soft stone that could be carved and hardened.

Many seals display an animal motif together with a short line of signs from the undeciphered Harappan script.

Frequently represented animals include bulls, elephants, rhinoceroses, tigers and buffaloes.

A particularly common motif is the unicorn, a stylised animal generally represented with a single visible horn.

Its exact symbolic meaning remains unknown.

Seals could serve practical purposes in marking goods and identifying their movement. Their symbolic designs might also have conveyed other meanings.

Consequently, the appearance of an animal on a seal does not by itself establish that the animal was worshipped.

The Pashupati or proto-Shiva seal

One of the most discussed Harappan seals was discovered at Mohenjodaro. It depicts a central seated figure surrounded by animals.

In the familiar interpretation, the figure appears horned and seated in a posture sometimes compared with a yogic position.

The surrounding animals include an elephant, tiger, rhinoceros and buffalo. Two smaller antelope-like animals appear beneath the seated figure.

Some scholars have identified the figure as Pashupati, meaning Lord of Animals, and interpreted it as an early representation of Shiva. For this reason, it is sometimes called the proto-Shiva seal.

However, this identification is disputed.

The figure's posture and association with animals do not establish its name or religious identity. NCERT also notes that the descriptions of Rudra in the Rigveda do not directly correspond to the combination of yogic and animal-associated characteristics attributed to the Harappan figure.

Alternative interpretations have therefore been proposed, including the possibility of a different religious or ritual figure.

The seal provides evidence of a significant symbolic representation, but it does not conclusively establish Shiva worship during the Harappan period.

Plant motifs and possible nature worship

Plants, trees and animal figures also appear in Harappan art.

Some seals contain tree or leaf motifs, including designs interpreted as resembling the pipal tree.

Such images have been interpreted as possible indications of reverence for nature or particular trees.

However, the precise symbolic meaning of these motifs is not known. A tree depicted on an object cannot automatically be identified as evidence of an established religious cult.

Other symbols and conical objects

Harappan objects also display geometric and symbolic designs, including the swastika motif.

The occurrence of such a symbol establishes its presence in Harappan material culture. It does not establish that the symbol possessed all the meanings associated with it in later religious traditions.

Some polished or conical stone objects were interpreted by early scholars as lingas, symbols associated with Shiva worship in later traditions.

However, their identification is uncertain. Similar objects could also have served other functions, including use as gaming pieces.

Why comparisons with later religion require caution

Religious practices sometimes change gradually, and later traditions may preserve elements of earlier beliefs. Therefore, comparisons between Harappan objects and later Indian religious symbols can be useful as possibilities.

Nevertheless, resemblance does not establish direct historical continuity.

The following distinctions are essential:

  • A female figurine is not automatically a confirmed Mother Goddess.
  • A seated horned figure is not automatically a confirmed representation of Shiva.
  • An animal motif does not automatically prove animal worship.
  • A tree motif does not automatically prove an organised tree-worshipping religion.
  • A conical stone object is not automatically a religious linga.

The Harappan script has not been deciphered, and the symbolic meanings of many images remain open to interpretation.

Prelims focus

  • Female terracotta figurines have sometimes been interpreted as Mother Goddess representations.
  • Harappan seals were commonly made from steatite.
  • The unicorn is a frequent motif on Harappan seals.
  • The Pashupati or proto-Shiva seal was discovered at Mohenjodaro.
  • The Pashupati seal shows a seated figure associated with several animals.
  • Plant, animal and geometric motifs occurred in Harappan material culture.
  • Trap: The Pashupati seal is not conclusive evidence of Shiva worship.

[Sources: NCERT, Class 12, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Theme 1, Sections 7.1 and 11.2, pp. 15 and 23–24; NCERT, Class 11, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Chapter 2, Arts of the Indus Valley, pp. 9–12; NCERT, Class 6, Exploring Society: India and Beyond, Chapter 6, pp. 99–101.]
